summary: High-potency first-generation antipsychotic used as an alternative option for severe Tourette tics and, off-label, delusional infestation. Effective for some people, but QT prolongation risk makes this a “respect the drug” medication.
description: Pimozide is a typical antipsychotic that can reduce severe motor and vocal tics in Tourette syndrome and is sometimes used off-label for delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis). It’s not usually tried first because of heart risk—especially QT prolongation (a heart-rhythm change that can be dangerous) that gets worse at higher doses—and because it can cause movement side effects (stiffness, shaking or restlessness), sleepiness, and drying side effects like dry mouth and constipation. ECG checks at the start and from time to time matter, and certain drug combinations must never be used.
patient_summary: Pimozide can help with severe Tourette tics and sometimes with delusional infestation, but it comes with real heart and movement-side-effect risks. You typically start low and raise the dose slowly, with ECG checks along the way. If your QT interval is long at the start or gets longer on treatment, lowering the dose or switching is often the right move. It needs close follow-up, and it’s not usually the first medicine tried for most people.

primary.context: FDA-labeled for suppression of severe motor and phonic tics in Tourette syndrome after inadequate response to standard treatments. Not intended as first choice.

off_label.context: Sometimes considered in tic disorders when other options are not accessible or not tolerated, but evidence quality is limited and QT risk changes the risk-benefit math.
Used as an alternative agent for delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis), typically reserved for situations where preferred options aren’t available or tolerated.

therapeutic_response.display: Within ~1 week for noticeable clinical effect (variable)

common_adverse_effects.notes: This can sneak up on you. Hydration, fiber, and a bowel plan matter—especially if you’re prone to constipation.
Many people feel slowed down, especially early on or after a dose increase. Bedtime dosing is often used to reduce daytime drag.
This can feel like anxiety but it’s different: more like your body can’t settle. If it happens, don’t just push through—tell your clinician.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Frequency not defined (can be clinically significant)
common_adverse_effects.notes: High-potency typical antipsychotics can cause stiffness and tremor. Dose adjustments and symptom management may be needed.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: 1% to 10% (ECG abnormalities reported); QT risk is dose- and interaction-dependent
common_adverse_effects.notes: This is why ECG monitoring exists in the first place. QT risk isn’t about how you feel—sometimes the ECG is the only early warning.

serious_risks.risk: Life-threatening heart rhythms (torsades de pointes) related to QT prolongation: fainting, palpitations, sudden collapse
A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS): fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, unstable heart rate and blood pressure
Severe movement reactions: sudden muscle spasms (dystonia), eyes locked upward (oculogyric crisis), or the back arching backward (opisthotonos)
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the tongue or face, that can become lasting)
Blood cell problems, including a dangerous drop in white blood cells (neutropenia), sometimes severe (agranulocytosis): fever, sore throat or signs of infection need urgent checking
Seizures (rare; risk higher in predisposed patients)

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to pimozide or any component
Severe toxic CNS depression or coma
A meaningfully long QT interval at the start, or conditions that make a dangerous heart rhythm (torsades de pointes) more likely
Concurrent use with QT-prolonging agents (contraindicated per labeling)
Hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia (must correct prior to initiation)

Taking medicines that strongly slow how your body breaks down pimozide (CYP3A4 inhibitors), such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, certain macrolide antibiotics and protease inhibitors, because levels rise and heart-rhythm risk goes up
Taking medicines that strongly slow its breakdown by another enzyme (CYP2D6 inhibitors), such as paroxetine, because levels rise and heart risk goes up
Use for simple tics or tics other than Tourette syndrome (contraindicated per labeling)

precautions: QT changes that grow with the dose: avoid using it if your QT interval (QTc, measured on an ECG) is already long at the start (a commonly used cutoff is above 450 msec), and don’t ignore QT increases during treatment
If the QT interval goes above 500 msec or rises a lot from the start (for example, by 60 msec or more), it needs urgent review: a lower dose or a switch to another antipsychotic
Must not be combined with many medicines that affect QT, or with medicines that strongly block the liver enzyme that breaks it down (CYP3A4 inhibitors), because of heart-rhythm risk

Movement side effects can occur, including muscle spasms (dystonia), a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), Parkinson-like stiffness and shaking, and tardive dyskinesia (lasting involuntary movements)
A rare but life-threatening reaction (neuroleptic malignant syndrome) can occur
Older adults: generally avoid (Beers Criteria concerns, including stroke/cognitive decline/mortality signals with antipsychotics in dementia-related psychosis)
CNS depression: can impair driving and tasks requiring alertness

interactions.mechanism: QT effects add up → risk of a dangerous heart rhythm (torsades de pointes).
interactions.action: Avoid combination. If a QT-prolonging drug is necessary, consider switching away from pimozide.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that strongly slow how your body breaks down pimozide (CYP3A4 inhibitors), such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, some macrolides and protease inhibitors
interactions.mechanism: Increased pimozide exposure → higher QT risk and toxicity.
interactions.action: The label says these must not be combined. Use a different antipsychotic or a different version of the other medicine.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that strongly slow pimozide’s breakdown by another enzyme (CYP2D6 inhibitors), such as paroxetine
interactions.mechanism: Increased pimozide levels → higher arrhythmia risk.
interactions.action: Avoid. If an antidepressant is needed, choose one that doesn’t create this high-risk interaction.

interactions.interactant: Some SSRIs that must not be combined with it or that affect QT (varies by medicine; the label lists several)
interactions.mechanism: Either QT synergy and/or metabolic inhibition depending on the specific antidepressant.
interactions.action: Treat this as a pharmacist-level interaction check every time. If you’re on pimozide, do not start or change antidepressants without reviewing interactions.

interactions.mechanism: Blocks the liver enzyme that breaks down pimozide → higher pimozide levels in the blood.

interactions.interactant: Electrolyte-lowering risks (anything that can cause low potassium or magnesium)
interactions.mechanism: Hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia increases torsades risk when QT is prolonged.
interactions.action: Correct electrolytes before starting and recheck when clinically indicated (vomiting/diarrhea, diuretics, etc.).

monitoring_requirements.parameter: ECG: Baseline and periodically thereafter, especially during dose adjustments, after significant dose increases, or when adding any QT-prolonging or metabolism-altering medication
Electrolytes (potassium, magnesium): Correct abnormalities prior to initiation; recheck when clinically indicated (diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, medical illness)

Genetic or other testing of how your body processes pimozide (CYP2D6 testing): at the start when higher doses are planned; required above certain doses (adult doses above 4 mg/day; for children, some guidance uses weight-based limits)

Movement side effects: a strong inner restlessness (akathisia), muscle spasms, and Parkinson-like stiffness—checked at every visit while the dose is being raised, with a structured scale from time to time if available
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements): checked regularly (every visit and at least once a year; more often if high risk)
Mental status and functioning: Track target symptom change (tics or delusional intensity), sedation, attention, and daily functioning
Blood count (CBC) when needed: especially if you have risk factors for low white blood cells; the medicine is stopped if ANC falls below 1,000/mm3
Vital signs and fall risk: Particularly in patients ≥60 or those with sedation/orthostasis symptoms
Weight/BMI and metabolic labs: While pimozide is not the most notorious for metabolic issues, antipsychotic monitoring standards still apply—especially if treatment is long-term
Therapeutic drug monitoring (when used): Draw trough just before next dose; interpret as an adherence and exposure tool rather than a standalone dosing target

special_populations.pregnancy: Use of antipsychotics in the third trimester can be linked to movement side effects and withdrawal symptoms in the newborn (agitation, muscle tone changes, tremor, feeding problems, breathing difficulty, sleepiness). Use only when the benefits clearly outweigh the risks, and coordinate with your pregnancy care team when possible.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known whether pimozide passes into breast milk. Because it could cause serious side effects in a nursing baby, weigh the importance of treatment against breastfeeding, and consider other treatment options when possible.
special_populations.geriatric: Generally avoid. Antipsychotics are flagged as potentially inappropriate in many older adults, especially for dementia-related behavioral symptoms. If used, justify carefully, use the lowest effective dose, and monitor closely for falls, cognitive effects, and cardiac risk.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution. Hepatic metabolism is clinically important, and drug interactions can meaningfully raise levels.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: At least 50% absorbed after oral dosing
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: mean ~111 hours (Tourette data); pediatric mean ~66 hours (6 to 13 years)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic N-dealkylation primarily via CYP3A4, with contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP2D6
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Avoid grapefruit juice due to increased serum concentration via CYP3A4 inhibition

dosing.titration: Pimozide dosing is slow-and-steady: start low, titrate carefully, and build in ECG monitoring—especially during dose changes. The dosing below reflects psychiatry-relevant uses from your notes (Tourette syndrome and delusional infestation).

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If pimozide needs to be stopped and it’s not an emergency safety stop, tapering is usually the move. A gradual taper helps you catch returning symptoms early and reduces the risk of withdrawal reactions (like agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, tremor, and restlessness).

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Pimozide is a first-generation antipsychotic that’s mainly used (in psychiatry practice) for severe Tourette tics when other options haven’t worked or aren’t tolerated. Off-label, it’s sometimes used for delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis), usually as an alternative option when preferred treatments aren’t accessible or tolerated. The big theme with pimozide is this: benefits can be real, but so is the cardiac risk—especially QTc prolongation—so monitoring and drug-interaction hygiene are non-negotiable.
items: {link:condition:tourette-syndrome:Tourette syndrome (severe motor and phonic tics)}: Alternative agent for significant functional impairment
{link:condition:delusional-infestation:Delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis)}: Off-label, alternative agent when preferred options aren’t available or tolerated

items.note: When it works, it often feels like less intensity and less frequency—not a full erase.

sections.intro: People’s experiences vary a lot, but pimozide tends to land in a few predictable buckets:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Pimozide is not an instant-relief medication. The goal is gradual symptom improvement with slow titration to keep side effects (especially cardiac and movement-related) under control.
key_points: Within ~1 week: Some people notice early change (often subtle)
4 to 6 weeks: Maximum effect may take this long to show up
6 to 8 hours: Time to peak blood level after a dose (range 4 to 12 hours)
Very long half-life: Effects and side effects can linger; dose changes may take time to fully “settle”

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Pimozide can reduce tics for some people, but current guidelines rate the confidence that it works better than placebo as low. In practice, the decision often comes down to: (1) how severe the tics are and how much they get in the way, (2) what’s already been tried, and (3) whether you can safely do the heart monitoring and avoid dangerous interactions.
sections.metric: Confidence in tic reduction vs placebo
sections.clinical_details: The American Academy of Neurology practice guideline on tics notes limited and lower-confidence evidence for pimozide’s benefit, and highlights the safety trade-offs—especially QT prolongation and extrapyramidal symptoms. That combination is why pimozide is typically reserved for more severe cases and for situations where other treatments are not effective or not feasible.

citation.title: Practice guideline recommendations: Treatment of tics in people with Tourette syndrome and chronic tic disorders

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Dose-dependent QTc prolongation can be dangerous. ECG monitoring and interaction avoidance are essential.
other: QT changes that grow with the dose: avoid using it if your QT interval (QTc, measured on an ECG) is already long at the start (a commonly used cutoff is above 450 msec), and don’t ignore QT increases during treatment
If QTc exceeds 500 msec or increases substantially from baseline (for example, ≥60 msec), reassess urgently: lower dose or switch antipsychotic
Contraindicated with many QT-prolonging drugs and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors due to arrhythmia risk
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), including dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia can occur
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is rare but life-threatening
Older adults: generally avoid (Beers Criteria concerns, including stroke/cognitive decline/mortality signals with antipsychotics in dementia-related psychosis)
CNS depression: can impair driving and tasks requiring alertness
patient_counseling: Get a baseline ECG and follow-up ECGs as recommended—especially during dose changes or if a new medication is added.
Do not combine pimozide with grapefruit juice. It can raise drug levels and increase QT risk.
Tell your prescriber about every med and supplement you take (especially antibiotics, antifungals, antidepressants, and anything that can affect QT).
If you faint, have palpitations, feel dizzy like you might pass out, or have new chest symptoms—treat that as urgent.
If you develop new restlessness, stiffness, tremor, tongue or facial movements, or severe fever/rigidity—contact a clinician immediately.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Pimozide is a typical antipsychotic, so the side effect profile is heavily weighted toward movement symptoms (EPS), sedation, and anticholinergic effects—plus the special concern: QT prolongation.

Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements (often tongue/face) that can become persistent
Blood dyscrasias including neutropenia/agranulocytosis: fever, sore throat, infection signs require urgent evaluation

sections.intro: Pimozide is the opposite of a “mix and match” medication. QT prolongation risk plus CYP metabolism means certain combinations are straight-up contraindicated.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If pimozide needs to be stopped and it’s not an emergency safety stop, tapering is usually the move. A gradual taper helps you catch returning symptoms early and reduces the risk of withdrawal reactions (like agitation, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, GI symptoms, tremor, and restlessness).
key_points: If treatment is ineffective or not tolerated, switching to another antipsychotic is often preferred over abrupt discontinuation in chronic psychiatric conditions
If you want to stop, lowering the dose gradually over weeks to months is commonly advised, to catch returning symptoms and reduce withdrawal reactions
If discontinuation is due to significant adverse effects (especially concerning ECG/QT changes), the risk-benefit may favor more rapid changes with close monitoring
Watch for withdrawal-style symptoms: agitation, anxiety, diaphoresis, dyskinesias, GI symptoms, insomnia, irritability, myalgia, paresthesia, tremor, vertigo, and rebound psychosis-like symptoms

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Pimozide dosing is slow-and-steady: start low, titrate carefully, and build in ECG monitoring—especially during dose changes. The dosing below reflects psychiatry-relevant uses from your notes (Tourette syndrome and delusional infestation).

adult.delusional_infestation_titration: Increase by 1 mg increments every 2 to 7 days based on response and tolerability
adult.delusional_infestation_max: Manufacturer labeling: max 10 mg/day or 0.2 mg/kg/day (whichever is less); doses up to 12 mg/day have been studied
adult.tourette_initial: 1 to 2 mg/day PO at bedtime or in divided doses
adult.tourette_titration: Increase as needed every other day based on response and tolerability
adult.cyp2d6_genotyping_threshold: If dose needs to exceed 4 mg/day, obtain CYP2D6 geno-/phenotyping before going higher
adult.cyp2d6_poor_metabolizer: Titrate in intervals ≥14 days; do not exceed 4 mg/day
adult.qt_adjustment_adult: If QTc prolongation is clinically significant (eg, QTc >0.52 seconds or >25% above baseline), decrease dose; if QTc is very prolonged (eg, >500 msec) or rises substantially from baseline, consider switching antipsychotics or lowering dose
adult.renal_impairment: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution
adult.hepatic_impairment: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution
adult.older_adult: Avoid use when possible (high-risk medication in older adults; use only with strong justification and close monitoring)

sections.simple_explanation: This med is titrated slowly because (1) side effects can show up with higher doses, and (2) QT risk is dose- and interaction-dependent. If the ECG starts to look risky, the correct response is usually dose reduction or switching—not ‘tough it out.’

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Pimozide needs extra caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, and in people with heart risk factors or electrolyte (blood salt) problems. Dosing also has limits based on genes (people who process it slowly, called CYP2D6 poor metabolizers).
sections.pregnancy: Antipsychotic exposure in the third trimester can be associated with newborn EPS and withdrawal symptoms (agitation, tone changes, tremor, feeding problems, respiratory distress, somnolence). Use only when the benefits clearly outweigh risks, and coordinate with obstetrics when possible.
sections.lactation: It is not known whether pimozide is excreted in breast milk. Because of potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant, weigh the importance of treatment against breastfeeding; consider alternative treatment strategies when feasible.
sections.geriatrics: Generally avoid. Antipsychotics are flagged as potentially inappropriate in many older adults, especially for dementia-related behavioral symptoms. If used, justify carefully, use the lowest effective dose, and monitor closely for falls, cognitive effects, and cardiac risk.
sections.hepatic: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution. Hepatic metabolism is clinically important, and drug interactions can meaningfully raise levels.
sections.renal: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution.

Electrolytes (potassium, magnesium): Correct abnormalities prior to initiation; recheck when clinically indicated (diuretics, vomiting/diarrhea, medical illness)
CYP2D6 geno-/phenotyping: At baseline when planning higher doses; required if exceeding specific dose thresholds (adult doses >4 mg/day; children thresholds are weight-based in some guidance)
EPS monitoring: Akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism—assess at every visit during titration; use a structured scale periodically if available
Tardive dyskinesia: Screen regularly (every visit and at least annually; more often if high risk)
Mental status and functioning: Track target symptom change (tics or delusional intensity), sedation, attention, and daily functioning
Blood count (CBC) when needed: especially if you have risk factors for low white blood cells; the medicine is stopped if ANC falls below 1,000/mm3
Vital signs and fall risk: Particularly in patients ≥60 or those with sedation/orthostasis symptoms
Weight/BMI and metabolic labs: While pimozide is not the most notorious for metabolic issues, antipsychotic monitoring standards still apply—especially if treatment is long-term
Therapeutic drug monitoring (when used): Draw trough just before next dose; interpret as an adherence and exposure tool rather than a standalone dosing target

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: In the US, pimozide is available as oral tablets. Dosing is typically once daily at bedtime or divided, depending on tolerability and symptom pattern.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Pimozide is a potent dopamine receptor antagonist (a high-potency typical antipsychotic). By blocking dopamine signaling in key brain circuits, it can reduce tic expression and can blunt fixed, false beliefs in delusional conditions for some patients—but that same dopamine blockade is why movement side effects (EPS, tardive dyskinesia) are a central risk.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Pimozide is usually a second- or third-line tool. For Tourette tics, it’s generally reserved for moderate-to-severe, function-impairing tics when standard treatments haven’t worked or aren’t tolerated—because QT risk and interactions raise the stakes. For delusional infestation, it’s typically considered an alternative option when preferred antipsychotics aren’t accessible or tolerated, and when the clinical picture is firmly in the delusional range (not a dermatologic or neurologic mimic).

faqs.q: What is pimozide used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry-focused use, pimozide is mainly an alternative option for severe Tourette tics when standard treatments haven’t worked or aren’t tolerated. Off-label, it can be used for delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis), usually as an alternative when preferred options aren’t available or tolerated.

faqs.q: Is pimozide usually the first medicine tried for Tourette tics?
faqs.a: Usually no. Because of cardiac risk (QT prolongation) and movement side effects, pimozide is typically reserved for more severe, impairing tics after other treatments have been tried.

faqs.q: Why does pimozide require ECG monitoring?
faqs.a: Because pimozide can prolong the QT interval in a dose-dependent way. QT prolongation can trigger dangerous heart rhythms. Baseline and follow-up ECGs help catch risk early—especially during dose changes or when new medications are added.

faqs.q: What heart-rhythm (QTc) numbers are considered concerning with pimozide?
faqs.a: Clinicians commonly avoid starting pimozide when the QT interval on the first ECG is already long (often referenced as above 450 msec). If it rises a lot on treatment (for example, a large increase from the start) or reaches very high levels (for example, above 500 msec), the usual next step is lowering the dose or switching to a different antipsychotic.

faqs.q: What medications should never be mixed with pimozide?
faqs.a: Many medicines that affect QT, and medicines that strongly block the liver enzyme that breaks down pimozide (CYP3A4 inhibitors), must not be combined with it, because they can raise pimozide levels and increase the risk of dangerous heart rhythms. Some antidepressants and antibiotics can also be problematic. Bottom line: don’t start, stop, or switch medicines while on pimozide without checking interactions.

faqs.q: Can grapefruit juice really be a problem?
faqs.a: Yes. Grapefruit juice can increase pimozide concentrations by inhibiting CYP3A4, which can increase QT risk. If you’re on pimozide, skip grapefruit.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects people notice?
faqs.a: Constipation, dry mouth, sedation/drowsiness, restlessness (akathisia), stiffness/tremor (EPS), and sometimes sexual side effects. The “special” risk is ECG changes (QT prolongation), which may not cause symptoms until it becomes dangerous.

faqs.q: What is akathisia — and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Akathisia — a medication side effect — feels like inner restlessness, like you can’t sit still. It can look like anxiety, but it’s more physical and urgent-feeling. It matters because it can be intensely uncomfortable and needs prompt attention, such as a dose or medicine change.

faqs.q: How long does pimozide take to work?
faqs.a: It’s not instant. Some people notice changes within about a week, but full effect may take several weeks (often cited as 4 to 6 weeks).

faqs.q: How do you stop pimozide safely?
faqs.a: Unless you’re stopping for a serious safety reason, lowering the dose gradually over weeks to months is usually recommended. That helps avoid withdrawal reactions and helps you spot returning symptoms early. If QT changes or other severe side effects show up, your prescriber may recommend a faster switch plan with close monitoring.

faqs.q: Is pimozide safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Often it’s best avoided. Antipsychotics are considered high-risk in many older adults, especially in dementia-related psychosis where increased mortality and stroke risks have been observed with antipsychotics as a class. If used, it should be with strong justification, the lowest effective dose, and tight monitoring.
